questions.problem:
The **exact** value of $c$ such that the average value of $f(x)=-15\sqrt{x}+6$ on the interval $[0,c]$ is equal to $-4$ is

$c=$
{{field-1}}.
questions.worked_solution:
To solve for $c,$ we apply the average value formula:

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{\text{avg}} & =\frac{1}{b-a}{\int }_{a}^{b}f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ -4 & =\frac{1}{c-0}{\int }_{0}^{c}(-15\sqrt{x}+6)\,\text{d}x \\ -4 & ={\frac{1}{c}(-10{x}^{3/2}+6x)|}_{0}^{c} \\ -4 & =\frac{1}{c}[(-10{c}^{3/2}+6c)-0] \\ -4 & =-10\sqrt{c}+6 \\ -10 & =-10\sqrt{c} \\ 1 & =\sqrt{c} \\ c & =1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the value of $c$ is 

$$
c=1.
$$

questions.worked_solution:
We need to use integration by parts. 

In this case, we define

$$
\begin{aligned}u={x}^{2}+3x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2x+3 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =({x}^{2}+3x)(-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))-\int (-\operatorname{cos}⁡(x))(2x+3)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x+3\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =-({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate $\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x.$ We take

$$
\begin{aligned}u=x\, & ⟹\,\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=1 \\ \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}=\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\, & ⟹\,v=\int \frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\text{d}x=\int \operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x=\operatorname{sin}⁡(x).\end{aligned}
$$

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\int x\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)\text{d}x & =\int u\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =uv-\int v\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x \\  & =(x)(\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))-\int (\operatorname{sin}⁡(x))(1)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)-\int \operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+D,\end{aligned}
$$

where $D$ is an integral constant.

So we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\int ({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)\,\text{d}x & =-({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2(x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+D)+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\  & =-({x}^{2}+3x)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+2x\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+C+3\operatorname{sin}⁡(x) \\  & =(-{x}^{2}-3x+2)\operatorname{cos}⁡(x)+(2x+3)\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)+C,\end{aligned}
$$

where $C=2D.$

questions.problem:
The subscriber count $P(t)$ of a streaming service follows the logistic growth model

$$
\frac{dP}{dt}=2P(5\,000-P),\,P(0)=300.
$$

where $t$ is the time, measured in years. For which value of $P$ is the subscriber count growing at the fastest possible rate?

$P=$
{{field-1}}
questions.worked_solution:
A logistic growth equation has the form

$$
{P}^{′}=kP(a-P),
$$

where $k>0$ is a constant of proportionality, and $a>P$ is the carrying capacity.

For a logistic growth model, the fastest rate of growth occurs when $P=\frac{1}{2}a.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14226573/assets/9019b26b417c757bbfab79afb39379c1fc7a892bc44e934c6f23c339deacfd68.png)

From our equation, we see that $a=5000.$ Hence, the carrying capacity is $5000,$ and $P$ grows at its fastest possible rate when 

$$
P=\frac{1}{2}a=\frac{1}{2}\cdot 5000=2500.
$$

questions.problem: Which of the following gives the arc length of the polar curve $r=\theta +{e}^{\theta }$ for $-\pi \le \theta \le \pi ?$
questions.worked_solution:
The arc length $L$ of a polar curve $r=r(\theta )$ is given by

$$
L={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r=\theta +{e}^{\theta },$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=1+{e}^{\theta }.
$$

Therefore, the arc length is

$$
\begin{aligned}L & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{(\theta +{e}^{\theta })^{2}+(1+{e}^{\theta })^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2\theta {e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }+1+2{e}^{\theta }+{e}^{2\theta }}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi }\sqrt{{\theta }^{2}+2{e}^{\theta }(\theta +1)+2{e}^{2\theta }+1}\,\text{d}\theta \,.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
In a factory, the average amount of sugar in a cookie is $15$ grams. However, $10%$ of cookies contain no more than $14$ grams of sugar. Assuming that the amount of sugar in each cookie is normally distributed, find the standard deviation of the amount of sugar in a cookie, rounded to $2$ decimal places.

*Hint: A table of values of ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ for different values of $p$ is given below, where $p=Φ(z)$ is the cumulative distribution function for the standard normal distribution. *

| $p$ | $\,0.01\,$ | $\,0.03\,$ | $\,0.05\,$ | $\,0.10\,$ | $\,0.15\,$ | $\,0.20\,$ | $\,0.25\,$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| ${Φ}^{-1}(p)$ | $\,-2.3263\,$ | $\,-1.8808\,$ | $\,-1.6449\,$ | $\,-1.2816\,$ | $\,-1.0364\,$ | $\,-0.8416\,$ | $\,-0.6745\,$ |
questions.worked_solution:
Let $X$ represent the amount (in grams) of sugar in a cookie. Then we have $X∼N(15,{\sigma }^{2}),$ and we want to find the standard deviation $\sigma .$ 

We know that $P(X\le 14)=0.10.$ Converting $X$ to a standard normal random variable by $z$-scoring, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 14) & =0.10 \\ P(Z\le \frac{14-15}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ Φ(-\frac{1}{\sigma }) & =0.10 \\ -\frac{1}{\sigma } & ={Φ}^{-1}(0.10).\end{aligned}
$$

From the table, 

$$
{Φ}^{-1}(0.10)=-1.2816.
$$

Finally then, 

$$
\begin{aligned}-\frac{1}{\sigma } & =-1.2816 \\ \frac{1}{\sigma } & =1.2816 \\ \sigma  & =\frac{1}{1.2816} \\  & ≈0.78.\end{aligned}
$$
